comment: I treated LN count as dominant, underweighting activation-dependent optimization: B and D’s rectifiers beat both GELU networks despite fewer LNs. Within activation groups, B’s normalization advantage over D and C’s over A correctly ordered them; zero-LN deep SiLU E remained last. K1006 was overextended; K1008 warned against a mandatory LN-first ordering. A plausible mechanism is stronger signal propagation through rectifiers at this small learning rate, not insufficient capacity. History: rectifiers won 3/3 equal-LN and 1/1 one-LN-deficit comparisons, but only 1/2 two-LN-deficit comparisons. Plain Adam-family lab comparisons supported a three-LN deficit in 2/2 sets, yet equal-LN higher-progress comparisons reversed in 2/2. These sparse, architecture-confounded checks do not validate a universal full-ranking rule.

    """One hidden layer: gelu(Linear(norm(x)))."""

    def __init__(self, width: int, use_layer_norm: bool) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(width) if use_layer_norm else nn.Identity()
        self.linear = nn.Linear(width, width)
        self.act = nn.GELU()

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
